Volume 12 · Chapter 06

Experiments and causal inference

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c05

By the endDesign and evaluate interventions with appropriate estimands and assignment mechanisms.

Volume 12 · Chapter 6

Experiments and causal inference

A public lender can randomize an offer, but cannot usually compel borrowing, prevent borrowers from sharing information, or force everyone to answer a later survey. The random draw establishes one part of an argument. A credible effect estimate also needs a defined intervention, a target population, an observation process and an inference procedure appropriate to the draw actually used. This chapter develops those pieces separately and then puts them together.

Capability. Derive finite randomization means and variances; distinguish sharp-null tests from average-effect inference; choose an allocation using an explicit power model; interpret encouragement estimates; handle a specified interference map; and establish sharp outcome bounds under attrition. All populations, samples and operational decisions below are original instructional constructions, not empirical findings.

Prerequisites. Identification and asymptotic tools supplies iid laws of large numbers, the finite-dimensional CLT and the delta method. IV and GMM supplies the binary compliance decomposition. Panel data and longitudinal identification distinguishes independent units from dependent rows and explains why a response mechanism needs its own assumptions. We prove the finite assignment results here. In particular, we do not obtain a finite-population normal approximation merely by writing a variance formula.

1. Name the intervention, the estimand and the random object

For now there are N named units. Unit i has two fixed potential outcomes Yᵢ(1) and Yᵢ(0), measured at a specified horizon in common outcome units. Treatment assignment Zᵢ∈{0,1} reveals Yᵢ=ZᵢYᵢ(1)+(1−Zᵢ)Yᵢ(0). This is consistency for the defined treatment versions, together with no interference: another unit's assignment does not change these two outcomes. Define τᵢ=Yᵢ(1)−Yᵢ(0) and the finite-population average τ̄=N−1∑τᵢ. An intervention effect differs from a comparison between people who selected treatment themselves.

Randomization means that the investigator knows a probability distribution over feasible assignment vectors. It does not mean that every vector has equal probability, that assignments are independent across units, or that observed outcomes are independent. Under complete randomization, exactly n₁ units are assigned treatment, n₀=N−n₁ control, and every size-n₁ subset has probability 1/choose(N,n₁). We require 1≤n₁≤N−1. The potential-outcome table is held fixed; only the assignment is redrawn.

Three probability laws used in this chapter
LawWhat is random?Target and valid reasoning
Fixed finite populationA vector drawn from a known assignment distributionEffect for these N units; exact assignment expectations, variances and sharp-null rank tests
Iid encouragement populationIndependent whole-unit potential vectors and independent encouragementsPopulation assignment or complier effect; iid score CLT and covariance-aware ratio inference
Known-Gaussian planning modelIndependent Gaussian observations within specified arms, with known variancesExact Gaussian test power at a stipulated population mean difference

The same difference of sample means can appear in all three rows, with different uncertainty. Conditioning an iid population on its realized potential table changes the probability law. A prospective calculation under known Gaussian variances is not a proof of exact Gaussian inference for six fixed units. Transport from the experimental population to other people or dates also requires assumptions beyond the assignment mechanism.

2. What fixed-count randomization proves

Write Ȳ(d)=N−1∑Yᵢ(d), Sd²=(N−1)−1∑[Yᵢ(d)−Ȳ(d)]², S10=(N−1)−1∑[Yᵢ(1)−Ȳ(1)][Yᵢ(0)−Ȳ(0)], and Sτ² analogously for τᵢ. These are descriptive finite-population quantities. Randomization expectation EZ integrates over assignments while keeping all these numbers fixed.

Inclusion moments. Counting subsets containing a given unit gives EZZᵢ=n₁/N=p. For distinct i,j, the corresponding count is choose(N−2,n₁−2), hence EZZᵢZⱼ=n₁(n₁−1)/[N(N−1)], including zero when n₁=1. Therefore VarZZᵢ=p(1−p) and CovZ(Zᵢ,Zⱼ)=−p(1−p)/(N−1). The negative covariance is a consequence of the fixed treatment count; it would be zero under independent Bernoulli assignment.

τ̂ = (1/n₁)∑ᵢZᵢYᵢ(1) − (1/n₀)∑ᵢ(1−Zᵢ)Yᵢ(0),
EZτ̂ = Ȳ(1)−Ȳ(0)=τ̄.

The equality follows term by term from the marginal inclusion probabilities. No constant treatment effect, Gaussian distribution, structural regression or random sampling of the N units was required.

Exact variance proof. Set cᵢ=Yᵢ(1)/n₁+Yᵢ(0)/n₀. The only random part of τ̂ is ∑Zᵢcᵢ. Applying the preceding covariance moments and using (∑cᵢ)²=∑cᵢ²+∑i≠jcᵢcⱼ gives

VarZ(∑Zᵢcᵢ) = [n₁n₀/{N(N−1)}]∑(cᵢ−c̄)²
= [n₀/(Nn₁)]S₁² + [n₁/(Nn₀)]S₀² + (2/N)S10
= S₁²/n₁ + S₀²/n₀ − Sτ²/N.

The last step uses Sτ²=S₁²+S₀²−2S10. Individual effects can be heterogeneous; their variation reduces this conditional design variance relative to the sum of the two arm terms. We usually cannot estimate Sτ² without additional information because each unit reveals only one potential outcome.

What the Neyman variance estimate guarantees. If both arm sizes are at least two, let sd² be the ordinary sample variance within observed arm d and V̂N=s₁²/n₁+s₀²/n₀. For any fixed list a₁,…,aN, its finite variance equals [N(N−1)]−1∑i<j(aᵢ−aⱼ)². For a uniformly selected size-m subset S, its sample variance is [m(m−1)]−1∑i<j; i,j∈S(aᵢ−aⱼ)². Each pair is included with probability m(m−1)/[N(N−1)], so taking expectations proves EZsd²=Sd². Consequently,

EZV̂N = VarZτ̂ + Sτ²/N ≥ VarZτ̂.

This is conservatism in expectation. It does not say that each realized V̂N exceeds the true design variance, or that τ̂±1.96√V̂N has any exact finite coverage. Normal approximation for a sequence of finite populations requires a separate theorem and conditions controlling influential units and nondegenerate variance. The scoped Ding text motivates this distinction; we use the finite results just proved, not an unproved finite-population CLT.

Worked case 1 · A conservative expectation with an anticonservative realization

For units numbered 0,…,5, set Y(0)=(0,1,2,3,4,5), τ=(0,2,0,2,0,2), hence Y(1)=(0,3,2,5,4,7). Randomize exactly three to treatment. There are 20 equiprobable assignments. Direct finite moments give τ̄=1, S₀²=7/2, S₁²=59/10, and Sτ²=6/5. Therefore

VarZτ̂ = (59/10)/3+(7/2)/3−(6/5)/6 = 44/15,
EZV̂N = 47/15.

If units 0,2,4 are treated, their observed outcomes are (0,2,4), and controls 1,3,5 reveal (1,3,5). The estimate is −1, both sample variances are 4, and V̂N=8/3, which is below 44/15. Enumerating all assignments verifies unbiasedness and the variance, but one observed randomization does not reveal its own estimation error.

A finite weak-average interval from known bounds. Suppose every Yᵢ(d) is known to lie in [ad,bd] before observing assignment, with range Rd=bd−ad. For a uniformly chosen index, (Y−a)(b−Y)≥0 gives E Y²≤(a+b)E Y−ab. Thus Var(Y)≤(E Y−a)(b−E Y)≤R²/4, and Sd²≤NRd²/[4(N−1)]. Dropping the nonpositive treatment-heterogeneity term gives the known upper bound

VarZτ̂ ≤ C = [N/{4(N−1)}](R₁²/n₁+R₀²/n₀).

For 0<α<1 and C>0, Chebyshev's inequality gives PZ(|τ̂−τ̄|≥√(C/α))≤α. The closed interval τ̂±√(C/α) therefore has coverage at least 1−α for the finite average, including heterogeneous effects. If C=0 the estimate equals the target surely. This can be very wide. With known ranges [0,5] and [0,7] in case 1, C=37/5, and the 90% halfwidth is √74. It is a proven finite bound, not a useful precision promise or a normal interval. Selecting ranges from observed maxima without a separate argument would invalidate the stipulated bound.

3. Sharp hypotheses, exact ranks and actual power

The sharp null H₀:Yᵢ(1)=Yᵢ(0) for every i imputes every missing potential outcome from the observations. The weak null τ̄=0 does not. Under a sharp null, fix an assignment-dependent statistic T(a), with large values chosen in advance to be unfavorable to the null. For a two-sided difference test use T=|τ̂|. Let Ω be the finite feasible assignment set and q(a)>0 its known probabilities, summing to one. The inclusive randomization p-value at observed a is

p(a)=∑b∈Ωq(b)1{T(b)≥T(a)}.

Finite weighted-rank proof. Group assignments with the same T value and order the groups from largest to smallest. Every assignment in group j has p-value equal to the cumulative probability of groups 1 through j. The event {p≤α} is a union of initial whole groups whose total mass is at most α. Hence PH₀(p≤α)≤α. This includes ties and unequal assignment weights; no continuity or asymptotic approximation is used. Replacing ≥ by > drops the observed tied group and can destroy validity. Exact size means control of the actual finite rejection probability, not equality to α for every design.

For the sharp constant-effect hypothesis Hc:Yᵢ(1)−Yᵢ(0)=c for all i, subtract cZᵢ from each observed outcome. If Hc is true, these adjusted values are the fixed untreated outcomes, so the same rank proof applies. Define the inverted set Cα={c:pc>α} when rejecting pc≤α. For a genuinely constant effect c₀, P(c₀∈Cα)≥1−α. This covers that sharp parameter. It is not automatically an interval for an arbitrary average under heterogeneous effects; those hypotheses impute different amounts of information.

Worked case 2 · A discrete test, a continuous inversion and nonmonotone small-design power

Retain Y(0)=(0,1,2,3,4,5) and three-of-six assignment, but now stipulate a constant true effect t. To compute power of the test of zero, for each actual assignment a generate observed outcomes Y(0)+ta. Then hold those outcomes fixed under the hypothesized zero effect, recompute |τ̂| over the twenty assignments, and reject if its inclusive p-value is at most α. This uses the actual alternative to generate data and the stated null procedure to analyze them.

Exact rejection probabilities for the sharp-zero test
True constant tα=1/10α=1/20
01/100
11/200
21/100
31/50
42/50

Complementary allocations have opposite mean differences and identical absolute statistics, so every inclusive p-value is at least 2/20. The α=1/20 test never rejects, even for the larger effects in the table. At α=1/10 its power at t=1 is below its size. Discreteness and the chosen two-sided rank procedure do not promise monotone power in this small design.

Now observe treatment of the last three units and Yobs=(0,1,2,5,6,7), giving difference 5. Under candidate c the adjusted list is (0,1,2,5−c,6−c,7−c), and the observed absolute difference is |5−c|. We can invert over all real c, without a parameter grid:

If c<3, each of the last three adjusted values exceeds each of the first three. The observed subset is the unique maximizing treated sum, and its complement the unique minimizing sum, so pc=2/20=1/10. If c>7, the order reverses with the same result. At c=3 the two middle values tie at 2; exchanging the tied units produces an additional maximizing subset and its complementary minimizer. The same happens at c=7 with a tie at 0. These endpoint p-values are 1/5.

For 3<c<5, the observed positive difference is not maximal: an untreated value 2 exceeds the smallest treated adjusted value 5−c. Exchanging them strictly increases the treated sum. For 5<c<7, the negative observed difference is not minimal: an untreated value 0 is below the largest treated adjusted value 7−c. Exchanging them strictly lowers that sum. Each case has at least the observed allocation, its complement, a more extreme allocation and its complement in the inclusive tail, hence pc≥4/20. At c=5 the statistic is zero and pc=1. Thus the exact acceptance set at α=1/10 is [3,7].

This observed table can arise with true constant t=2, so that true value can be excluded in a tail realization. Coverage is a repeated-assignment statement. Neither the set's center nor rejection of a sharp zero hypothesis establishes that every individual benefits.

4. Strata and clusters change the assignment information

Partition the fixed population into preassignment strata h=1,…,H of sizes Nh, and independently randomize exactly n1h and n0h within each, both positive. Let τ̄h be the stratum finite average and τ̂h its treated-minus-control mean. The whole-population target is τ̄=∑whτ̄h, where wh=Nh/N. The corresponding estimator and variance follow from the finite proof and independence of the stratum draws:

τ̂S=∑whτ̂h,
EZτ̂S=τ̄,
VarZτ̂S=∑wh²[S1h²/n1h+S0h²/n0h−Sτh²/Nh].

Using weights based only on the realized numbers treated instead targets a different mixture when treatment fractions differ. Strata formed after inspecting treatment outcomes also lack this prospective assignment justification. The stratified randomization treatment is used only in this independent, fixed-stratum scope.

Worked case 3 · Blocking removes a specified source of imbalance

Eight units have Y(0)=(0,1,2,3,10,11,12,13) and constant treatment effect 2. Under complete four-of-eight assignment, there are 70 assignments, S₀²=S₁²=30, and variance 15. Under independent two-of-four assignment in each of the low and high baseline strata, there are 36 assignments. Each stratum has S₀²=S₁²=5/3, hence contrast variance 5/3. Weighting each stratum by 1/2 gives

VarZτ̂S = (1/2)²(5/3)+(1/2)²(5/3) = 5/6.

Both estimators have expectation 2. In this population, blocking prevents large baseline differences between the arms while preserving within-stratum comparisons. This specific gain does not prove that every stratification rule or every allocation improves every estimand's variance.

Cluster assignment. If an entire school or branch receives one assignment, its constituent rows do not become independent randomization units. A cluster-level potential outcome can be its mean outcome. Applying the finite proof to clusters then targets the average of those cluster means, provided no between-cluster interference affects that definition. With unequal cluster sizes, this is generally different from the mean effect across people; the target and weights must be specified. More rows in the same dependent cluster cannot be counted as more independent draws. Section 5 gives a fully specified Gaussian cluster calculation rather than asserting a generic clustered normal theorem.

5. Power is a calculation under an alternative model

Consider a separate planning law. Independently sample n₁ Gaussian outcomes in arm 1 with mean μ₁ and known variance σ₁²>0, and n₀ independent Gaussian outcomes in arm 0 with mean μ₀ and known variance σ₀²>0. All arm observations are mutually independent. Then D=Ȳ₁−Ȳ₀ is exactly N(δ,v), with δ=μ₁−μ₀ and v=σ₁²/n₁+σ₀²/n₀. At two-sided size α, reject δ=0 if |D|/√v>z, where z=Φ−1(1−α/2). Equality has probability zero here.

Power(δ;n₁,n₀)=Pδ(D/√v>z)+Pδ(D/√v<−z)
=Φ(λ−z)+Φ(−λ−z),   λ=δ/√v.

Φ is the standard normal CDF. Both tails are retained. For δ>0, derivative with respect to λ is φ(λ−z)−φ(λ+z)>0 because (λ+z)²−(λ−z)²=4λz>0. The power is symmetric in the sign of δ. Thus at a fixed nonzero effect and total N, minimizing v maximizes power.

Allocation proof. With continuous n₁=Np and n₀=N(1−p), the objective is v(p)=[σ₁²/p+σ₀²/(1−p)]/N. Its derivative vanishes when σ₁/p=σ₀/(1−p), so p*=σ₁/(σ₁+σ₀). The second derivative is strictly positive for 0<p<1, proving the unique global minimum v*=(σ₁+σ₀)²/N; the objective diverges at both endpoints. For integer n₁, the same strict convexity means only the floor and ceiling of Np*, restricted to 1,…,N−1, can minimize variance. Compare those two actual values; rounding p* once for every N need not choose the best allocation. Adding an observation to either arm strictly decreases variance, so the best attainable variance decreases with total N.

Worked case 4 · A defensible minimum sample size

Use σ₁²=9, σ₀²=1, δ=1, α=.05 and target power .8. The continuous optimum assigns fraction 3/4 to treatment, giving variance coefficient 16/N; equal allocation gives 20/N. The exact two-tail calculation and the neighboring integer comparisons are:

Known-variance planning at the minimum-size boundary
NTreatment/controlVariancePower, rounded
12594/31373/29140.798168
12694/32191/15040.801270
156, equal78/785/390.797546
158, equal79/7910/790.802541

The best variance decreases with N. The best N=125 design is below target and N=126 reaches it, so 126 is the minimum total for unrestricted integer allocation. If equal integer arms are required, totals are even; the corresponding minimum is 158. These minima depend on the known variances, the effect size, both tails and the stated design freedom. Estimated variances, unequal costs, attrition or a different outcome law require new calculations.

A proved cluster transfer. Suppose there are twenty independent Gaussian clusters, ten assigned to each arm, each containing m=10 observations Ygj=μd+Ag+εgj. The common cluster shocks A have variance 1; idiosyncratic shocks ε have variance 4; all shocks are centered independent Gaussian variables except for the sharing of A within a cluster, and assignment is independent of these shocks. Cluster means have known variance 1+4/10=7/5. The difference of the two averages of ten cluster means is Gaussian with variance 7/25. Treating the hundred rows per arm as independent would instead give 1/10.

In general, with common variance σA² and idiosyncratic variance σε², the ratio of the correct contrast variance to the independent-row calculation for equal cluster sizes is 1+(m−1)ρ, where ρ=σA²/(σA²+σε²). Here ρ=1/5 and the variance multiplier is 14/5; the standard-error multiplier is its square root. This follows by summing the common and averaged idiosyncratic components. It does not require pretending that a cluster covariance estimator is known or Gaussian. The randomization toolkit motivates the design tradeoff; the exact Gaussian contract here is narrower than general field-experiment planning.

6. Randomizing an offer identifies an assignment effect

Now use an iid population of whole units. Each has binary treatment potentials D(0),D(1), and encouragement Z is independently drawn with fixed probability p∈(0,1), independently across units and independently of their full potential vectors. Let YZ(z) denote the outcome under assignment z, including any direct assignment channel and the treatment it induces. With consistency and no interference, observed Y=YZ(Z), D=D(Z). Randomization identifies the intention-to-treat effect ΔY=E[Y|Z=1]−E[Y|Z=0]=E[YZ(1)−YZ(0)], whether or not encouragement has a direct effect. It also identifies γ=E[D|Z=1]−E[D|Z=0].

A treatment-effect interpretation of β=ΔY/γ requires more. Impose exclusion YZ(z)=Y(D(z)) for two treatment outcomes Y(0),Y(1); independence of Z from (D(0),D(1),Y(0),Y(1)); integrable outcomes; monotonicity D(1)≥D(0); and positive complier probability γ=P(D(1)>D(0))>0. Then

ΔY=E[(Y(1)−Y(0))(D(1)−D(0))]
=γ E[Y(1)−Y(0)|D(1)>D(0)],

so β is the local average treatment effect for compliers. Always-treated and never-treated people contribute zero to the assignment contrast. This is the accepted Imbens–Angrist compliance argument from c03. It does not make β the population ATE or the effect among everyone treated. Exclusion and monotonicity are distinct from random assignment and cannot be inferred from a positive average first stage.

Random-arm means and their signed influence. Assume iid observed triples with finite E Y²; D is binary. Write μYz=E[Y|Z=z], μDz=E[D|Z=z], p₁=p, p₀=1−p and p̂z=n−1∑1{Zᵢ=z}. On the event that both arms are nonempty,

μ̂Yz−μYz = {n−1∑1{Zᵢ=z}(Yᵢ−μYz)}/p̂z.

LLN gives p̂z→pz>0. The numerator is a centered iid average with finite second moment, so the CLT and inverse continuity give the influence ψYz=1{Z=z}(Y−μYz)/pz. The analogous treatment influence replaces Y with D. Let ψY=ψY1−ψY0 and ψD=ψD1−ψD0. For fixed γ≠0, consistency and the exact ratio identity give

√n(β̂−β) = (1/γ)n−1/2∑[ψYi−βψDi]+oP(1),
Vβ = [VY+β²VD−2βCYD]/γ²,
VY=EψY²,   VD=EψD²,   CYD=EψYψD.

The covariance term is essential because the outcome and treatment contrasts use the same people. These are variances of the root-n limits; the estimator variance is approximated by Vβ/n. The proof applies to the ratio target even without a LATE interpretation. Empty-arm probability is pⁿ+(1−p)ⁿ, which tends to zero. LLN and γ≠0 also make the event of a zero estimated first stage asymptotically negligible. Assigning an arbitrary value on such exceptional samples is a mathematical convention for a limit proof; software should report that the ratio is undefined. No uniform approximation as γ approaches zero is claimed.

Feasible variance. Replace each arm mean, p, β and γ in the influence by its consistent sample estimate and average its square. On events where fitted denominators are bounded away from zero, subtracting fitted from true influences is bounded by a vanishing coefficient times a constant multiple of 1+|Y|. LLN for 1+Y² therefore makes the average squared difference oP(1). Cauchy–Schwarz controls the cross term, while the true squared influence has an integrable LLN. The resulting variance estimate is consistent. Studentization additionally requires Vβ>0. This is an iid whole-unit argument, not the fixed-table variance in Section 2.

Worked case 5 · The complier effect and the covariance that accompanies it

Each independent unit has a type drawn from this table, and receives independent fair encouragement P(Z=1)=1/2. Treatment outcomes do not depend directly on Z.

Original compliance population
TypeShareD(0),D(1)Y(0),Y(1)
Never treated1/20,01,7
Always treated1/81,12,6
Complier3/80,13,5

Treatment means under Z=0,1 are 1/8 and 1/2; outcome means are 19/8 and 25/8. Thus γ=3/8, ΔY=3/4, and β=2. The population ATE is (1/2)6+(1/8)4+(3/8)2=17/4. The actually treated share is 1/8+(1/2)(3/8)=5/16; its average treatment effect is [(1/8)4+(3/16)2]/(5/16)=14/5. Specifying the encouragement probability is necessary for this treated mixture.

Enumerating the six type-by-assignment states gives VY=235/16, VD=23/32 and CYD=97/32. Therefore

Vβ=[235/16+4(23/32)−4(97/32)]/(3/8)²=116/3.

An independent check uses Q=Y−2D. It equals 1,4,3 for the never, always and complier types respectively, regardless of Z. Its mean is 17/8 and variance 87/64. Fair assignment makes the contrast influence variance 4 Var(Q)=87/16; dividing by γ² gives the same 116/3. Omitting outcome–treatment covariance instead gives 1124/9. That error can materially change uncertainty even when the point estimate is computed correctly.

7. Interference requires outcomes indexed by a defensible exposure

Under interference, write Yᵢ(a) for unit i's outcome under the complete assignment vector a. An exposure map eᵢ(a) compresses that vector into a label. Using exposure-level potential outcomes Yᵢ(h) assumes that any two feasible assignments with eᵢ(a)=eᵢ(b)=h give the same outcome for unit i. A network label is not self-validating: distant assignments, treatment intensity or versions may matter even if the chosen label omits them.

For a known assignment distribution define πᵢ(h)=P(eᵢ(Z)=h), and πᵢⱼ(h,k)=P(eᵢ(Z)=h,eⱼ(Z)=k), including i=j. Suppose the map is correct and πᵢ(h)>0 for every unit in the target. The Horvitz–Thompson exposure-mean estimator is

μ̂HT(h)=(1/N)∑ᵢ 1{eᵢ(Z)=h}Yᵢobs/πᵢ(h),
EZμ̂HT(h)=(1/N)∑ᵢYᵢ(h)=μ(h).

On the indicated event, correct mapping makes the observed outcome equal to Yᵢ(h); taking the indicator expectation cancels πᵢ(h). This proves unbiasedness without independence between unit exposures. For a contrast τ=∑h∈Hahμ(h), apply linearity to τ̂=∑ahμ̂HT(h). Expanding its variance using pairs of indicators gives the exact formula

VarZτ̂ = (1/N²)∑i,j∑h,k∈HahakYᵢ(h)Yⱼ(k)
×[πᵢⱼ(h,k)−πᵢ(h)πⱼ(k)]/[πᵢ(h)πⱼ(k)].

Positive marginal probabilities suffice for these estimators. They do not make every joint probability positive: one unit cannot simultaneously have two distinct exposures, and two neighbors may be unable to attain certain exposures together. If πᵢⱼ(h,k)=0, an observed-product estimator cannot recover Yᵢ(h)Yⱼ(k) by dividing a joint indicator by that zero probability. A full synthetic potential table permits an oracle variance calculation, but one experiment generally does not reveal every product in it. The Aronow–Samii framework supports this finite mapping and inclusion-probability scope; no general large-network limit theorem is imported.

Worked case 6 · A path of three units

Units 0–1–2 form a path. Independently assign each a fair binary treatment. Define eᵢ=(Dᵢ,Gᵢ), where Dᵢ is own assignment and Gᵢ indicates any treated neighbor. Stipulate the full synthetic outcome table by Yᵢ(d,g)=bᵢ+τᵢd+3g, with b=(1,2,3), τ=(2,4,6). The target is the average effect of changing own treatment while holding neighbor exposure at zero:

τ10,00=(1/3)∑ᵢ[Yᵢ(1,0)−Yᵢ(0,0)]=4.

For each endpoint, exposures (0,0) and (1,0) have probability 1/4. For the middle unit both neighbors must be untreated, so each probability is 1/8. Use a10=1 and a00=−1 in the HT contrast. For example assignment 000 gives (1/3)(−4·1−8·2−4·3)=−32/3. Assignment 010 exposes only the center to (1,0), giving (1/3)(8·6)=16.

Full exact assignment distribution of the HT contrast

0001/8−32/3

Averaging gives 4 and exact variance 688/9. The joint-inclusion formula gives the same variance. Adjacent units cannot both have exposure (1,0): each would require its treated neighbor to be untreated. This zero joint probability does not invalidate their positive marginal means, but it prevents direct observation of that cross-exposure product.

If the design instead treats exactly one uniformly selected unit, the center can never have exposure (0,0). The full-population contrast then lacks the required marginal positivity and cannot be recovered by this HT construction. Without an additional outcome restriction, changing the center's missing Y₁(0,0) leaves that design's observable law unchanged while changing the target. The stipulated full table above still lets us calculate an oracle target; knowing or extrapolating its additive formula is extra information, not a consequence of the new assignment design.

8. Random assignment does not randomize survey response

Let R(d)∈{0,1} indicate whether outcome Y(d) would be observed under assignment d. Suppose assignment is independent of the joint potential vector (Y(0),Y(1),R(0),R(1)), with positive probabilities for both arms, no interference and consistency. Observe R=R(Z) and Y only if R=1. In a population law, let rd=P(R=1|Z=d)>0 and md=E[Y|Z=d,R=1]. These observed means describe responders under each assignment, who need not be the same people. They need not equal the full arm means.

If Y(d)∈[Ld,Ud] is a known substantive restriction, write the unobserved nonresponse mean as ud∈[Ld,Ud]. Total expectation gives E Y(d)=rdmd+(1−rd)ud. Therefore

τ ∈ [r₁m₁+(1−r₁)L₁−r₀m₀−(1−r₀)U₀,
r₁m₁+(1−r₁)U₁−r₀m₀−(1−r₀)L₀].

This is a population identification interval from bounded missing outcomes. It uses no missing-at-random assumption. If an arm has rd=0, its respondent mean is undefined and its full mean is simply bounded by [Ld,Ud]; it should not be represented by a fictitious observed mean. Sampling estimates of response rates and means bring additional uncertainty, so plugging them into this formula is not by itself a confidence procedure.

Worked case 7 · Equal response rates, opposite substantive conclusions

Outcomes lie in [0,10]. Both arms respond with probability 4/5; treatment responders have mean 8 and control responders mean 6. The treatment population mean lies in [32/5,42/5], and the control mean in [24/5,34/5]. The resulting sharp ATE interval is

[−2/5,18/5],

which contains zero despite a respondent difference of 2. To prove sharpness rather than just calculate inequalities, construct potential responses R(0),R(1) as independent Bernoulli(4/5) variables. This independence is a convenient endpoint construction, not an identification assumption. The masses for (R(0),R(1))=(1,1),(0,1),(1,0),(0,0) are respectively 16/25,4/25,4/25,1/25.

Whenever R(1)=1 set Y(1)=8, and whenever R(0)=1 set Y(0)=6. For the lower endpoint set Y(1)=0 when R(1)=0 and Y(0)=10 when R(0)=0. For the upper endpoint reverse these missing-value endpoints: Y(1)=10 and Y(0)=0. Draw assignment independently of the full constructed vector. Both constructions have exactly the same observed law: the same response probability and a point mass at 8 or 6 among the corresponding responders. Their population effects are −2/5 and 18/5. A mixture of the two constructions, mixed independently of assignment, preserves the observed law and attains every intermediate effect. Thus no smaller interval follows from these observations and bounds alone.

Equal response rates do not prove equal response identities, independent response or absence of selection on unobserved outcomes. Follow-up measurement, credible outcome restrictions, or a justified response model can improve identification. They must be stated and defended; random assignment alone supplies none of them. The toolkit's attrition discussion motivates this threat; the endpoint construction here is original and does not invoke a trimming theorem.

9. Design the analysis before the outcome arrives

A useful protocol starts with the intervention version, outcome definition, horizon, target population and assignment unit. Write the assignment probability law, including strata, counts and any restrictions. Specify the estimand and which missing outcomes its identification requires. Then choose an estimator and uncertainty statement proved for that law. The intended number of rows is not enough to establish any of these.

Record noncompliance, potential direct assignment channels, plausible spillovers and response mechanisms prospectively. If possible, collect exposure and follow-up information that distinguishes competing mechanisms. Keep a primary contrast and test statistic fixed before inspecting outcomes; the rank proof for one chosen statistic does not automatically cover selecting the most favorable of many analyses. A larger sample can reduce sampling noise under the correct law but cannot by itself identify an excluded counterfactual or fix an incorrect exposure map.

Report assignment effects even when the treatment-received interpretation needs additional qualifications. Explain whether an interval is an exact sharp-parameter inversion, a finite bound on a weak average, an iid asymptotic interval, or a population identification region. These objects answer different questions. Code can validate the promised arithmetic and design support; it cannot establish that participants experienced the intended treatment versions or that an exclusion restriction is substantively true.

Exercises

The twelve prompts are original. Supply assumptions alongside calculations. Proof questions require a valid argument; the finite tables are opportunities to check it, not substitutes for it.

  1. Under complete n₁-of-N assignment, derive E Zᵢ and E ZᵢZⱼ for i≠j by counting subsets. Prove unbiasedness of the difference in means and its exact design variance, including the sign of the treatment-heterogeneity term. State what changes under independent Bernoulli assignment with the same marginal p.
  2. Prove unbiasedness of each sample arm variance using pairwise differences, and explain why the resulting Neyman estimate need not dominate the design variance in a realized sample. Recompute the realized assignment 0,2,4 in case 1. Then derive the known-range Chebyshev interval and its 90% halfwidth for that case; explain why substituting observed ranges or a normal critical value is not justified by that proof.
  3. Prove the inclusive weighted-rank p-value inequality for a finite nonuniform assignment law. For three assignments with probabilities (1/2,1/4,1/4) and null statistics (2,2,0), compute every inclusive p-value and the rejection probability at α=1/4. Repeat using a strictly greater tail and diagnose the error. Explain why a weak average-zero null does not generally permit the sharp-zero imputation.
  4. For the observed last-three-treated data in case 2, prove analytically that the constant-effect inversion at α=1/10 is [3,7]. Explain both endpoints and the center. Describe how to compute the power table under t=0,1,2,3,4 and why no α=1/20 rejection is possible. Does exclusion of the true constant 2 in this observation contradict the coverage proof?
  5. In case 3, keep the two strata and all potential outcomes but assign one treated unit in the low stratum and three in the high stratum, independently. Calculate the expectation and design variance of the correctly weighted estimator. Calculate the expectation of the naive pooled treated-minus-control mean. Explain why this change affects the estimand of the pooled calculation and why usual sample arm variance estimates are unavailable in some cells.
  6. Derive the exact two-sided Gaussian power formula, the optimal continuous allocation and the floor/ceiling integer rule. For case 4 verify the allocations and powers immediately below and above each minimum-size boundary. Give a proof that these boundary checks establish the minima. State three design or distribution changes that would require recalculation.
  7. Derive the cluster-mean and treatment-contrast variances for Section 5's twenty-cluster Gaussian model. Derive the general equal-size design factor using the common and idiosyncratic variances, and distinguish the standard-error factor. Explain the limits as the common component is zero and as the number of observations within each existing cluster grows without increasing the number of clusters. What target issue arises with unequal cluster sizes?
  8. Derive the random-arm mean influence and the ratio influence under the iid encouragement contract, including the empty-arm and zero-first-stage qualifications. Recompute case 5's covariance-aware root-n variance using Q=Y−2D. Now add a direct outcome increment Z/2 while leaving the treatment potentials unchanged. Find the ITT and Wald ratio, and explain which treatment interpretation fails.
  9. Derive exposure HT unbiasedness and its joint-inclusion variance formula. Recompute case 6's assignment table, mean and variance. Identify a zero joint probability and explain why knowledge of the full synthetic table permits a variance calculation that a single observed experiment generally does not.
  10. Change case 6's independent assignment probability to a common p∈(0,1). Derive the marginal probabilities of exposures (0,0) and (1,0) for endpoints and the center. Explain the failure under fixed-one-of-three assignment. Separately add 2Z₂ to unit 0's outcome while retaining its old exposure label; exhibit two assignments showing why that label is no longer sufficient.
  11. Derive the bounded-outcome population ATE interval in Section 8. For case 7 construct two full potential-outcome/response laws with the same observed distribution that attain its endpoints, and prove attainability of all intermediate values. Explain why equal response rates and a narrow sampling standard error for respondent means do not remove the identification problem.
  12. A research team assigns twenty branches, ten per arm, an encouragement to adopt a credit-screening tool. It reports 200 client rows, uses the independent-row known-Gaussian power calculation with variances estimated after the trial, calls a treatment-received regression the population ATE, finds equal 80% follow-up in each arm, and permutes client labels to test the most favorable of twelve outcomes. Branches exchange recommendations. Write a referee-style design and analysis repair. Address the probability law, randomization unit, estimand, compliance, interference, missing outcomes, analysis selection and the difference between power and observed uncertainty. Provide concrete evidence requests rather than automatically accepting or rejecting the intervention.

Solutions and proof checks

Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The single-unit count is choose(N−1,n₁−1), divided by choose(N,n₁), giving n₁/N. For a distinct pair it is choose(N−2,n₁−2), giving n₁(n₁−1)/[N(N−1)]; when n₁=1 there are no such subsets. Subtracting p² gives Cov(Zᵢ,Zⱼ)=−p(1−p)/(N−1). Applying the marginal moments to the two sample means gives E τ̂=Ȳ(1)−Ȳ(0).

    Write τ̂=∑Zᵢcᵢ−∑Yᵢ(0)/n₀ with cᵢ=Yᵢ(1)/n₁+Yᵢ(0)/n₀. The covariance expansion is p(1−p)[∑cᵢ²−∑i≠jcᵢcⱼ/(N−1)]=n₁n₀∑(cᵢ−c̄)²/[N(N−1)]. Expanding the square yields n₀S₁²/(Nn₁)+n₁S₀²/(Nn₀)+2S10/N. Substitution of Sτ²=S₁²+S₀²−2S10 gives S₁²/n₁+S₀²/n₀−Sτ²/N. The heterogeneity term is subtracted because the two counterfactual lists share unit identities and the assignment count is fixed.

    Under independent Bernoulli assignment, E Zᵢ stays p but E ZᵢZⱼ=p² and pair covariance is zero. The realized arm counts are random and can be zero. Dividing by fixed expected counts yields an HT-type estimator, whereas dividing by actual counts gives random ratios. The fixed-count algebra cannot be carried over unchanged to either uncertainty calculation. The treatment fraction alone does not specify the design.

  2. For m selected values, ∑i<j(aᵢ−aⱼ)²=m∑(aᵢ−ā)², so s² is that pair sum divided by m(m−1). Each population pair enters a simple random size-m sample with probability m(m−1)/[N(N−1)], making E s² the population pair sum divided by N(N−1), namely S². Both arm sizes must be at least two. Then E V̂N−Var(τ̂)=Sτ²/N≥0, an expectation inequality only. In the specified assignment, observed arm means are 2 and 3; τ̂=−1, each arm sample variance is 4 and V̂N=8/3<44/15.

    For Y∈[a,b], (Y−a)(b−Y)≥0 implies Var(Y)≤(E Y−a)(b−E Y)≤(b−a)²/4. Uniform indexing over the finite table converts this to S²≤NR²/[4(N−1)]. Dropping −Sτ²/N gives C=N[R₁²/n₁+R₀²/n₀]/[4(N−1)]. Chebyshev and unbiasedness give coverage at least 1−α for τ̂±√(C/α), with the zero-variance case exact. Here C=6(49/3+25/3)/20=37/5, so at α=.1 the halfwidth is √74, approximately 8.602325. The known bounds refer to all counterfactual outcomes, not just observed extrema; using the latter may underestimate the range. The proof uses Chebyshev, not a Gaussian pivot, so changing its critical factor to 1.645 would need another theorem.

  3. Order distinct statistic levels from largest to smallest and let their positive total assignment masses be w₁,…,wk. Every assignment in level j has inclusive p-value Wⱼ=∑ℓ≤jwℓ. Those with Wⱼ≤α form an initial union of levels of total probability at most α. This proves the inequality without assuming equal weights or distinct statistics.

    For the stated example, the two tied upper assignments have inclusive p-values 3/4, and the lower assignment has p=1. At α=1/4 the rejection probability is 0. Strictly greater tails instead give p=0 for both upper assignments and p=3/4 for the lower one, so their rejection probability is 3/4, violating the proposed 1/4 level. The weak average-zero null permits positive and negative individual effects and does not reveal each missing potential outcome. Holding all observed outcomes fixed as though every effect were zero therefore need not generate the actual weak-null distribution.

  4. The adjusted list is (0,1,2,5−c,6−c,7−c) with observed absolute mean difference |5−c|. For c<3 the observed last-three subset is the unique top-three subset; for c>7 it is the unique bottom-three subset. Only it and its complement are as extreme, giving p=.1 and rejection under the stated ≤ convention. At c=3 or 7 a tied middle value can be swapped across arms, giving two extreme subsets and their complements, so p=.2 and acceptance.

    For 3<c<5, replacing treated value 5−c by control value 2 increases the positive contrast. For 5<c<7, replacing treated value 7−c by control value 0 makes the negative contrast more negative. The observed subset and its complement plus the more extreme pair give p≥.2. At c=5, |5−c|=0 and every allocation is in the tail. This covers the entire real line and proves C.1=[3,7].

    For each true t and each of twenty actual assignments a, generate yobs=y₀+ta, compute the twenty zero-null absolute contrasts, count those at least as large as the actual one, and then count rejection across the actual assignments. The rejection counts at α=.1 are 2,1,2,4,8, yielding the printed powers. Complementary assignments always tie in absolute contrast, so every p≥2/20 and no α=.05 rejection is possible. Excluding true t=2 in one realization is allowed; the proof bounds its total rejection probability under repeated assignment, not the correctness of every set in isolation.

  5. The target stratum weights remain 1/2 each. Constant effect 2 gives each stratum contrast expectation 2. Each stratum still has S₁²=S₀²=5/3, and now contrast variance (5/3)(1+1/3)=20/9. Independent draws therefore give weighted mean 2 and variance (1/4)(20/9+20/9)=10/9. There are 16 possible assignments.

    The expected treated mean is [(1)(3/2+2)+(3)(23/2+2)]/4=11. The expected control mean is [(3)(3/2)+(1)(23/2)]/4=4. Their difference is 7. It adds 5 of baseline composition difference to the common effect 2. One treated observation in the low stratum and one control in the high stratum do not support ordinary within-cell sample variances with denominator m−1. The known full potential table still permits exact design variance calculation; a real observed sample would need another justified variance strategy. Weighting by target populations solves the estimand mismatch, but does not create missing variance information.

  6. Independent known-variance Gaussian means make D/√v distributed N(λ,1). Its upper rejection tail is 1−Φ(z−λ)=Φ(λ−z); its lower tail is Φ(−z−λ). Their sum gives the formula, symmetric in δ. For λ>0, differentiation gives φ(λ−z)−φ(λ+z)>0. Thus minimize v=σ₁²/n₁+σ₀²/(N−n₁). Its derivative vanishes at n₁=Nσ₁/(σ₁+σ₀), and its second derivative 2σ₁²/n₁³+2σ₀²/(N−n₁)³ is positive. On either side it is monotone toward this point, so an integer minimum lies among its adjacent integers.

    For N=125 compare n₁=93 and 94; 94 gives variance 373/2914 and power .798168. For N=126 compare 94 and 95; 94 gives 191/1504 and power .801270. Giving any extra observation to either arm of a previous optimum strictly lowers variance, so the optimized variance strictly decreases with N. The two boundary checks prove minimum N=126. For equal allocation the possible totals are even; 78 per arm gives .797546, while 79 gives .802541, proving minimum 158. These are rounded displays of exact Gaussian CDF calculations.

    Changing the stipulated effect or target size/power changes the noncentrality/critical value; estimating variances changes the reference law; costs or allocation caps change the optimization; clustering changes the variance; and differential missingness changes both effective data and possibly the estimand. Any three clearly justified examples receive credit. The calculation cannot infer the true effect from observed significance.

  7. A cluster average is μd+Ag+m−1∑εgj, with variance σA²+σε²/m. Averaging J independent clusters per arm and subtracting gives 2(σA²+σε²/m)/J for equal variances. The erroneous independent-row calculation is 2(σA²+σε²)/(Jm). Their ratio is (mσA²+σε²)/(σA²+σε²)=1+(m−1)ρ. With m=J=10, σA²=1 and σε²=4, the two variances are 7/25 and 1/10, the variance factor 14/5 and the standard-error factor √(14/5), approximately 1.673320.

    With no common component, the factor is one. With a positive common component and fixed J, m→∞ leaves contrast variance 2σA²/J; observing more people within existing clusters does not remove their common shocks. Unequal sizes make the equally weighted average cluster effect differ from the person-weighted effect unless further conditions align them. A proposed weighting rule needs a target and an assignment-based proof. Exact Gaussian calculations here use known shock variances; neither many rows nor estimated variances alone establish that pivot.

  8. On nonempty arms, μ̂Yz−μYz=Eₙ[1{Z=z}(Y−μYz)]/p̂z. LLN and pz>0 allow replacement of the inverse denominator, while the finite-second-moment iid CLT yields ψYz=1{Z=z}(Y−μYz)/pz. Use the joint CLT for these and D analogues. With Δ̂Y−βγ̂=(Δ̂Y−ΔY)−β(γ̂−γ), division by γ̂ gives influence (ψY−βψD)/γ. Squaring it retains −2βCov(ψY,ψD). Its variance must be positive for ordinary studentization.

    Empty-arm probability pⁿ+(1−p)ⁿ tends to zero, and consistency with fixed γ≠0 makes a zero or very near-zero fitted denominator asymptotically exceptional in this fixed-parameter theorem. A finite implementation must still reject undefined ratios. There is no uniform weak-first-stage conclusion.

    For case 5, Q equals (1,4,3) with masses (1/2,1/8,3/8), so E Q=17/8 and E Q²−(E Q)²=87/64. The fair-arm contrast influence is 2(2Z−1)(Q−17/8); its variance is 4(87/64)=87/16. Dividing by (3/8)² yields 116/3. Adding Z/2 changes ΔY to 5/4 and the ratio to 10/3. The complier treatment effect at fixed encouragement remains 2, and γ remains 3/8. Assignment randomization still identifies the new ITT, but exclusion fails because the encouragement itself changes the outcome. The ratio now mixes that direct channel with treatment uptake and is not this LATE.

  9. Correct mapping implies 1{eᵢ=h}Yᵢobs=1{eᵢ=h}Yᵢ(h). Taking expectation and dividing by positive πᵢ(h) gives Yᵢ(h), proving HT unbiasedness after averaging. In the square of the contrast, E[1{eᵢ=h}1{eⱼ=k}]=πᵢⱼ(h,k). Subtracting the squared mean gives the stated signed double sum, including i=j and different exposures.

    For the path under independent fair assignments, endpoints need their own binary value and one untreated neighbor, so π=1/4 for each target exposure; the center also needs its other neighbor untreated, so π=1/8. Substituting observed outcomes gives (−32/3,32/3,16,0,0,16,0,0) in lexicographic assignment order. Their mean is 4, and their mean square is 832/9. Subtracting 16 gives 688/9. Adjacent units cannot both be treated with no treated neighbor, so π₀₁((1,0),(1,0))=0. More basically, a single unit cannot occupy (1,0) and (0,0) simultaneously.

    The finite variance identity is an oracle expression in all potential outcomes. The supplied synthetic formula gives those values, enabling its exact evaluation and agreement with direct enumeration. In an actual experiment the corresponding unobserved products are generally unknown, and a zero joint probability rules out obtaining them by a simple inverse-joint-probability observed-product average. Positive marginal support alone is not a guarantee of an unbiased observable estimator for the full variance.

  10. For an endpoint, no treated neighbor has probability 1−p, independently of its own assignment. Hence π(0,0)=(1−p)² and π(1,0)=p(1−p). For the center both neighbors must be zero, giving π(0,0)=(1−p)³ and π(1,0)=p(1−p)². All are positive for 0<p<1; endpoints p=0 or 1 eliminate required exposures.

    Under fixed-one-of-three assignment, the center is either treated itself or has a treated neighbor, so π₁(0,0)=0. An estimator for the full contrast cannot divide by this probability. In the model class with unrestricted exposure potential outcomes, changing only Y₁(0,0) produces the same observed law and a different contrast. If one assumes the full additive formula and all coefficients known, the target is already given by that extra information; randomization did not identify the missing cell.

    For the mapping change, compare assignments 000 and 001. Unit 0 has own treatment 0 and neighbor treatment 0 in both, so its old exposure is (0,0). Its augmented outcomes are 1 and 3 because the distant unit 2 changes. Equal labels no longer imply equal outcomes. One must enrich the map or change the target/model; calculating old inclusion probabilities cannot repair the omitted spillover.

  11. Under independent assignment and consistency, the full arm mean is rdmd+(1−rd)ud, where ud is the nonrespondent potential-outcome mean. The outcome bounds constrain ud to [Ld,Ud]. Minimize the treatment mean and maximize the control mean for the lower effect endpoint; reverse these choices for the upper endpoint. This yields the displayed interval without assuming response independence.

    For the example, construct the four potential-response cells with probabilities 16/25,4/25,4/25,1/25. In both endpoint laws reveal Y(1)=8 whenever R(1)=1 and Y(0)=6 whenever R(0)=1. For the lower law put missing Y(1)=0 and missing Y(0)=10, producing means 32/5 and 34/5 and effect −2/5. For the upper law put missing Y(1)=10 and missing Y(0)=0, producing means 42/5 and 24/5 and effect 18/5. Independent assignment yields identical observable distributions (Z,R,Y when observed) under both laws. Mixing them with any weight in [0,1], independently of assignment, preserves this law and interpolates their effects linearly. This proves sharpness and attainability, not merely outer bounds.

    The same response fraction can select different people or outcomes in the two arms. Even infinitely many observations could reveal the respondent law perfectly while leaving both endpoint constructions possible. Sampling precision for observed means therefore does not resolve this missing-counterfactual uncertainty. A justified response model, additional follow-up or stronger outcome restrictions may narrow it, but requires separate evidence.

  12. Illustrative referee response and open rubric. Request the actual branch assignment list, probabilities, fixed counts and any strata or restrictions. A branch is the assignment unit; client permutations violate that design. A valid sharp-null randomization calculation should draw feasible branch assignments with their known weights and state what null imputes the missing outcomes. Dependence among clients must remain in the chosen variance or outcome aggregation. Two hundred rows alone do not supply two hundred independent draws.

    Define the primary outcome, horizon, intervention version and whether the target is an average across branches or across clients. Report the randomized encouragement ITT. A regression on treatment received is affected by selection unless another argument identifies it. A LATE interpretation of an encouragement ratio requires exclusion, monotonicity, a nonzero first stage and the specified complier population; ask about direct information or funding channels, uptake patterns and who can respond. A population ATE or transport claim needs additional assumptions.

    Document recommendation sharing and candidate exposure maps, check design support for the desired contrast and consider a revised assignment/measurement plan. Do not assume that a branch boundary eliminates interference. Request follow-up rates, identities and outcome bounds; equal 80% response does not establish missing at random. Show a sensitivity or identification interval, and distinguish its sampling uncertainty from the missing-outcome uncertainty.

    Disclose all twelve outcomes and how the favorable one was selected. The one-statistic rank proof does not automatically validate the selected test; a prospective primary outcome or a separately justified selection/multiplicity procedure is needed. The chapter does not claim a particular generic correction solves every selection rule. Finally, power is a prospective probability under a stipulated alternative and variance law. Estimated post-trial variances do not equal the known variances required by the exact Gaussian planning formula; confidence statements need a method justified for their own observation and assignment law. Request the original effect-size, variance, attrition and cluster assumptions, and recompute design sensitivity before another trial.

    Full credit requires all eight named issues, a correct separation of estimands and probability laws, and at least one specific evidence request or design repair for each unresolved identification or inference claim. Alternative justified designs earn credit; a policy recommendation must weigh costs, potential harms, uncertainty and the actual target rather than demand a predetermined sign or significance result.

Teach-back and retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why “the intervention was randomized” does not by itself establish a population ATE with a normal confidence interval. Use one finite-design equation, one compliance distinction and one missing-outcome or interference construction. The aim is a coherent argument from design to target to uncertainty, not a list of cautions.

Teach-back benchmark

A satisfactory explanation names what was assigned and to whom, states the random object and target, and derives at least the inclusion-probability unbiasedness identity. It distinguishes the finite variance S₁²/n₁+S₀²/n₀−Sτ²/N from an iid ratio influence or a known-Gaussian power law. It explains that assignment ITT survives a direct encouragement channel while LATE needs exclusion and monotonicity. It then gives a concrete ambiguity: equal-response laws with effects −2/5 and 18/5, or a missing center exposure under fixed-one-of-three assignment. A precise sharp-null rank or Chebyshev conclusion is better than an unsupported normal approximation. No claim about transport or all individual effects should be inferred from the average alone.

Retention check. Without reopening the examples, answer four questions. (a) If a finite design has V̂N below the true variance in one draw, which proved statement can still hold? (b) With twenty equiprobable balanced assignments and a complement-symmetric absolute statistic, can an inclusive p-value be .05? (c) If m rises while ten independent clusters per arm retain common variance 1 and idiosyncratic variance 4, what is the limiting contrast variance? (d) If the only newly measured outcomes in case 7 are the treatment-arm nonrespondents, all equal to 4, what is the revised ATE identification interval while control nonrespondents remain unobserved?

Retention answers

(a) EZV̂N=VarZτ̂+Sτ²/N still holds; it is an average over assignments. (b) No: the observed assignment and its distinct complement tie, so the inclusive p-value is at least 2/20=.1. (c) The idiosyncratic average vanishes, leaving 2·1/10=1/5. (d) The treatment mean becomes (4/5)8+(1/5)4=36/5, while the control mean remains between 24/5 and 34/5. The effect interval is [2/5,12/5]. Actual additional outcomes narrow identification; equal original response rates did not.

Sources and limits of the argument

The three new primary routes are Peng Ding's A First Course in Causal Inference, arXiv version 2 dated 3 October 2023; Aronow and Samii's general-interference paper, retrieved arXiv version 4 dated 20 June 2018, distinct from its 2017 journal reference; and Duflo, Glennerster and Kremer's Using Randomization in Development Economics Research: A Toolkit, the inspected January 2007 CEPR discussion-paper version. The source record reuses the coordinator's exact body and equation-page inspections and the accepted c03 compliance source scope. It does not claim a fresh full-document inspection by this author. All numerical populations, power calculations, endpoint constructions, exercises and solutions here are original.

We proved finite complete and stratified randomization moments, expected Neyman conservatism, a known-range finite weak-average bound, inclusive sharp-null ranks and constant-effect inversion, exact known-Gaussian power and allocation, a fixed-first-stage iid ratio expansion, exposure HT mean/variance identities and bounded-outcome attrition sharpness. We did not prove a finite-population CLT, a generic cluster or large-network asymptotic theorem, weak-first-stage uniform inference, a general multiplicity correction, missing-at-random from observed response rates, or transport to another population. Code checks finite arithmetic and stated domains; substantive design assumptions require evidence from the intended intervention. The next chapter develops difference-in-differences and event studies, where treatment timing and counterfactual trends require their own identification arguments.

Sources and further study

  • A First Course in Causal Inference — Finite complete-randomization assignment moments, exact difference-in-means variance and expected Neyman variance; independent stratified weighted variance; separate superpopulation versus randomization perspectives. Prior accepted v05-c12 sharp-null rank scope physical51–55/printed25–29 is reused honestly.
  • Estimating average causal effects under general interference, with application to a social network experiment — Known randomization distribution and exposure mapping; individual and joint exposure probabilities; positive support and correctly specified exposure-level potential outcomes; HT mean unbiasedness and finite covariance expansion.
  • Using Randomization in Development Economics Research: A Toolkit — Design/power tradeoffs, group assignment and independent cluster information, compliance and attrition; equal response rates need not remove selection bias.
  • Guido W. Imbens, Joshua D. Angrist — Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects (Econometrica62(2), March1994, pages467–475) — Binary heterogeneous treatment effects, compliance decomposition and LATE limits. Original finite population and violations are not attributed to the paper.
